intro: These are the questions every student asks when they first work through DNS enumeration. Each one reveals a genuine gap between how most people think DNS works and how it actually works in practice.

faqs.question: Is DNS enumeration legal to perform on a company without their permission?
faqs.answer:
Querying public DNS records is entirely legal and requires no permission. When you run a dig query or use an online DNS lookup tool, you are sending queries to public DNS resolvers (like 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1) — not to the target's own systems. The DNS records you receive are public by design; the internet cannot function if they are not publicly accessible. You are reading information that the organisation published, using a system that any device on the internet uses constantly.

The one important exception is zone transfer (AXFR): this query goes directly to the target's nameserver, creates a log entry on their server, and is an active technique. Zone transfer attempts require written authorisation as part of a professional engagement scope agreement. The passive DNS enumeration techniques — querying all record types through public resolvers — require no authorisation and leave no trace on the target's systems.

faqs.question: How is DNS enumeration different from port scanning? They both seem like they're looking for what a server is running.
faqs.answer:
They are fundamentally different in three ways: what they look at, how they work, and what authorisation they require.

DNS enumeration queries public DNS records — information the organisation published and that lives on public nameservers. Nothing reaches the target's actual servers. No logs are created on their systems. It is entirely passive. No authorisation required.

Port scanning (Nmap and similar tools) sends packets directly to the target's IP addresses and listens for responses. Every packet reaches the target's systems. Every scan creates log entries. It is active. It always requires written authorisation.

DNS enumeration tells you what services an organisation RUNS based on their own public declarations. Port scanning tells you which ports on which IP addresses are currently open and responding. They answer different questions. In a professional engagement, DNS enumeration comes first — it tells you which systems are worth scanning, so that port scanning is targeted rather than speculative.

faqs.question: What happens if I accidentally find a security issue during passive DNS enumeration — like a dangling CNAME pointing to a deleted service — on a company I wasn't authorised to test?
faqs.answer:
This happens regularly in security research. The discovery itself is legal — you found it by reading public DNS records, which anyone can do. The question is what you do next.

If the company has a bug bounty programme: review the programme scope and determine whether this type of finding is covered. If it is, submit the finding through the official programme. Do not claim the deleted cloud resource or serve any content from it — that would cross the line into exploitation, which is not authorised.

If the company has no bug bounty programme: you have two legitimate options. First, do nothing — the finding is not your responsibility to resolve for a company you have no relationship with, and moving on is entirely reasonable. Second, attempt responsible disclosure — contact the company's security team (usually through their security.txt file or abuse@ email address) to report what you found, with no expectation of reward and no threat of disclosure.

What you must never do: claim the deleted cloud resource, serve content from it, or attempt to exploit the configuration in any way without explicit written authorisation. Even if you intended no harm, doing so would almost certainly constitute unauthorised access under computer fraud laws.

faqs.question: Why do TXT records accumulate over time and never get cleaned up?
faqs.answer:
Because TXT records have no expiry mechanism, no automatic validation, and no central audit process. When a company connects a new cloud service to their domain, the provider asks them to add a specific TXT record to prove domain ownership. The DNS administrator adds it. The service is activated. And then: nothing. There is no notification when the service is later discontinued. There is no automatic removal. The TXT record sits in DNS indefinitely — until someone specifically goes looking for it and removes it.

This is compounded by organisational dynamics. The person who added the record was probably a developer or IT administrator setting up the service. The person who cancelled the service years later was probably on a finance or procurement team. Neither knows about the other's DNS records. In large organisations, hundreds of TXT verification tokens can accumulate over years — a complete history of every cloud service the company has ever tried, documented in their public DNS zone.

faqs.question: If zone transfers are dangerous, why does the feature exist at all? Why not just remove it from DNS entirely?
faqs.answer:
Zone transfers are a legitimate and necessary feature of DNS infrastructure. Every domain should have multiple nameservers for reliability — if the primary nameserver goes offline due to a network failure, hardware fault, or attack, secondary nameservers continue answering DNS queries. For secondaries to have accurate records, they need a way to synchronise with the primary. Zone transfer is that synchronisation mechanism.

The feature itself is not dangerous. The misconfiguration is dangerous: allowing zone transfer requests from any IP address rather than only from authorised secondary nameservers. A properly configured nameserver only responds to zone transfer requests from IP addresses specifically listed as authorised secondaries. Most modern DNS hosting providers configure this correctly by default.

Where the misconfiguration appears: older self-managed nameservers configured in an era when DNS security was less mature, administrators who set up nameservers years ago and never reviewed the configuration, or internal DNS servers that were never intended to face the internet but ended up exposed due to network architecture changes.
